title: The Academy Gazette Scoop
covers: how to write a whole number as a product of prime numbers with a factor tree, and how to write that product with exponents
cert: building factor trees and writing prime factorizations with exponents

intro.caption: Lesson 6-13 — prime factorization. The Academy Gazette needs a front page by morning. A secret tip is on its way, and Vale's rival paper wants it too. Three gates and a boss press stand between the Gazette and its scoop.

balloons.t: The Gazette needs a scoop. Something big. Something TRUE.
Tip from the old archive! The door opens with the prime factorization of 72.

pages.caption: 8 and 9 are not prime. They are composite, so they can still split. A factor tree keeps going until every branch ends in a prime.

balloons.t: Warm-up: 36. Keep splitting until every branch is prime.
The press prints prime numbers only. Feed it a composite and it jams.
My paper says 1 is prime. Front page. Try to keep up.
The headline has room for exponents. Not for 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
Two trees for one number give two answers. Everybody knows that.
Three plates left on the press. Get all three right.
Headline: 72 = 2³ × 3². Vale's paper: still says 1 is prime.

win.caption: A factor tree splits a number until every branch ends in a prime. 1 is not prime, so it never ends a branch. Any tree for the same number ends in the same primes, and exponents write the product short.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Grow the Tree
gates.prompt: Teo's tree for 36 stops at 4 × 9. Finish it.
hints: Conceptual: a branch can stop only at a prime number. A composite number can still split into smaller factors.
Procedural: look at each end of the tree. Can you split it into two numbers bigger than 1? If yes, keep going.

steps: 5 is prime, so that branch stops. 4 is composite, so split it: 4 = 2 × 2.
Every branch now ends in a prime: 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.

items.q: Teo's tree for 36 ends at 4 and 9. What is wrong?

options.fb: 4 × 9 is 36, but 4 and 9 are composite. A tree stops only at primes.

options.t: 4 and 9 are composite, so both must keep splitting.

options.fb: 1 × 36 never gets smaller. 1 is not prime, so it does not help the tree.
9 = 3 × 3, so 9 is composite. It must split too.

fb.msg: 2 × 2 × 3 × 9 = 108, not 36. And 9 is composite: it splits into 3 × 3.

items.fbDefault: 4 = 2 × 2 and 9 = 3 × 3. Which prime is still missing?

gates.pass: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Every branch ends in a prime. Teo calls his first tree "a rough draft."

gates.title: Gate 2 · The Prime Press
gates.prompt: The press prints prime numbers only. Sort the numbers before they jam the gears.
hints: Conceptual: a prime number is bigger than 1 and has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 1 has only one factor.
Procedural: try to divide by 2, 3, 5 and 7. If one goes in evenly (and is not the number itself), it is composite.

steps: The primes at the ends are 2, 3 and 5. Check: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30.
worked.q: Which primes end the tree for 14?

items.q: Which numbers can the press print? Pick all the primes.

options.fb: Yes: 2 has exactly two factors, 1 and 2.
9 = 3 × 3, so 9 is composite.
1 has only ONE factor. A prime needs exactly two, so 1 is not prime.
Yes: only 1 and 5 go into 5.
21 = 3 × 7, so 21 is composite.
Yes: only 1 and 11 go into 11.

items.fbMiss: You missed a prime. Check each number: does anything besides 1 and itself go in?
items.fbExtra: One of your picks jams the press. Is it composite, or is it 1?

items.q: Ozzie runs 42 through the press. Which primes come out?

options.fb: 6 is composite (2 × 3). The press jams. Keep splitting.
1 is not prime. Leave it out.
21 is composite (3 × 7). Keep splitting.

gates.pass: 2, 5, 11 print clean. 42 comes out as 2, 3 and 7. Vale's 1 jams the press, just like it jams her front page.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Write It Short
gates.prompt: The tree for 72 ends in 2, 2, 2, 3 and 3. Write the headline with exponents.
hints: Conceptual: an exponent tells how many times a factor is multiplied. 2 × 2 × 2 is 2³.
Procedural: count how many 2s and how many 3s. Write each prime once, with its count as the exponent.

steps: Practice: the tree for 24 ends in 2, 2, 2 and 3.
There are three 2s, so write 2³. There is one 3, so write 3.

items.q: Which is the prime factorization of 72?

options.fb: 8 × 9 is 72, but 8 and 9 are composite. This is Teo's first try.
That's 4 × 27 = 108. The exponents are swapped: there are three 2s and two 3s.
12 is composite. Split it into 2 × 2 × 3.

items.label: 2³ × 5 =
items.aria: the value of two cubed times five

fb.msg: 30 is 2 × 3 × 5. The exponent 3 means 2 × 2 × 2, not times 3.
2³ = 8, but then multiply by 5. You added.

gates.pass: 72 = 2³ × 3². Short enough for the front page — and every factor is prime.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Stop the Presses
gates.prompt: Three plates are left on the press. Each one must be a true prime factorization.
hints: Conceptual: a prime factorization uses only primes, never 1 and never a composite. Any tree for a number ends in the same primes.
Procedural: build the tree, list the primes at the ends, then count them for the exponents. Multiply back to check.

steps: Each 10 = 2 × 5, so the ends are 2, 5, 2 and 5.

items.label: Plate 1 · 2 × 3² × 5 =
items.aria: the value of two times three squared times five

fb.msg: That's 2 × 3 × 5. You left out the exponent: 3² means 3 × 3.

items.q: Plate 2 · Which is the prime factorization of 84?

options.fb: 4 and 21 are composite. Split them: 4 = 2 × 2 and 21 = 3 × 7.
1 is not prime, so it never goes in a prime factorization.
42 is composite. Keep splitting it.

items.q: Plate 3 · Vale prints: "A tree for 48 that starts 6 × 8 and one that starts 4 × 12 give different answers." True?

options.t: True. Different first splits give different primes.
options.fb: Finish both trees. 6 × 8 and 4 × 12 both end in 2, 2, 2, 2 and 3.

options.t: True. One tree can end at 1.
options.fb: 1 is not prime, so no finished tree ends at 1.

options.t: False. 48 is prime, so it has no tree.
options.fb: 48 is even, so 2 goes into it. 48 is composite.

gates.pass: KA-CHUNK. Three true plates: 90, 2² × 3 × 7, and 2⁴ × 3 from any tree. The archive door opens, and the Gazette has its scoop.

journal.heading: Lesson 6-13 — what the Gazette scoop taught us
rows: A prime number is bigger than 1 and has exactly two factors, like 2, 3, 5 and 7. A composite number has more, like 9 = 3 × 3. 1 is neither.
Split a number into factors and keep splitting every composite branch. Stop only when every branch ends in a prime: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
72 = 8 × 9 is true, but 8 and 9 are composite. Stopping early is not a prime factorization. Any finished tree for 72 ends in the same primes.
journal.quote: "If it still splits, it's not news yet." — Chip

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 6-13 (Prime Factorization) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: prime and composite numbers, why 1 is not prime, building factor trees until every branch is prime, and writing the prime factorization with exponents.
standards: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers ≤ 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers ≤ 12
